detail.longDescription: I am building a commercial REST API using AWS API Gateway backed by a Node.js origin (via VPC Link and an Internal NLB). I am using API Gateway API Keys and Usage Plans to manage customer quotas and rate limits. My product has two tiers: Standard: Access to all core endpoints. Premium: Access to all core endpoints, plus one specific restricted endpoint ( GET /premium-query ). The Goal I want all customers to use a single, unified Base URL (e.g., [api.example.com/v1](https://api.example.com/v1) ). If a Standard customer upgrades to Premium, the /premium-query endpoint should simply unlock for their existing API key without requiring them to migrate to a new URL. If a Standard customer hits the restricted endpoint, they should receive a clear 403 Forbidden response indicating they need to upgrade. The Problem Natively restricting a single route to specific Usage Plans on a single stage while maintaining correct HTTP semantics is proving difficult. I have evaluated three standard approaches, and all have fatal flaws for my use case: Multiple API Gateway Stages: Bind Standard keys to a std stage and Premium keys to a premium stage, enforcing access natively. The flaw: The Base URL changes depending on the customer's plan. Upgrades require code changes on the client side, which is a terrible developer experience. Method-Level Throttling (Rate Limit: 0): Keep everyone on one stage, but configure the Standard Usage Plan with a method-level throttle of 0 for the /premium-query endpoint. The flaw: API Gateway natively returns a 429 Too Many Requests instead of a 403 Forbidden . Standard customers will assume they exhausted their monthly quota. It also triggers infinite retry loops in standard HTTP clients. Origin-Side Control Plane Lookup: Pass the x-api-key-id to the Node.js origin, and have the origin call apigateway:GetApiKey to check the associated Usage Plan before serving the request. The flaw: This introduces AWS Control Plane calls into the data path. The API Gateway management APIs have strict rate limits (around 5 RPS). A cache miss during a traffic spike will throttle the origin and cause cascading 500 errors. Gemini's Proposed Solution: S3-Pushed Allowlist To keep everything on a single stage and return proper 403s without hitting control plane limits, I am considering decoupling the authorization state via S3: The Writer: Whenever a subscription changes via Stripe webhooks, my provisioning service generates a JSON array of all Premium API Key IDs and overwrites a file in an S3 bucket. The Reader: My Node.js origin polls this S3 object in the background every 60 seconds using conditional GETs (ETag). It caches the allowed keys in memory using a JavaScript Set . The Guard: When a request hits /premium-query , the origin checks the incoming x-api-key-id header against the memory cache. If it is not found, the origin instantly returns a 403 Forbidden with a custom JSON error instructing them to upgrade. My Questions: Is this S3 background polling approach a recognized architectural pattern for bridging API Gateway Usage Plans with origin-side route authorization? I am fairly new to enterprise API builds, so would love to get feedback on this. Any alternatives without complicating the build? Thank you!
